title: Observe and review the design
summary: Use metrics, logs, and traces to understand a service. Check a small error-rate calculation, then review a design with clear evidence.
introduction: A library manager cannot fix a long queue by guessing. They count visitors, watch waiting time, and ask where work gets stuck. A computer service needs useful signals in the same way.
learningObjectives: Tell a metric, a log, and a trace apart
Calculate an error rate and describe its limits
Use evidence to review a slow or failing design

rows: 5 failed searches out of 100 requests in one minute
Request r52 could not reach the catalog database
The timed steps of one request
r52 spent 10 ms in the API and 400 ms waiting for the database

blocks.text: **Observability** means being able to understand what a system is doing from its signals. We need more than a green light saying the server process is running. People may still be unable to search.
Our sample has five made-up requests. Four succeed and one fails. A request takes some number of milliseconds, written ms. One second is 1,000 milliseconds.

blocks.title: Small JavaScript model
blocks.caption: This model uses made-up values in your browser. It does not contact a service.

blocks.content:
requests: 5
failures: 1
error percent: 20
successful average ms: 100
blocks.title: Expected output

blocks.text: The error rate is 1 divided by 5, then multiplied by 100: 20 percent. The successful requests take 400 ms in total, so their average is 400 divided by 4: 100 ms.
This sample is tiny. It does not prove what a busy service will do. We labelled the average as successful requests only. Failures still matter and must stay visible in a separate measure.
Choose measures that answer a question

items: Traffic: how many requests arrive in a chosen time window?
Errors: what share of requests fail? Keep the total beside the rate.
Latency: how long do people wait? Check slow requests as well as the average.
Capacity: how full are worker queues, memory, and connections?

blocks.text: A **percentile** helps show slow requests. The 95th percentile is a time at or below which about 95 out of 100 measured requests finish. It can reveal slow waits hidden by an average.
Review one problem step by step

items: Start with the user problem: searching is slow, or borrowing fails. Pick the matching measure and time window.
Compare with a normal period. Check how much traffic changed, not just how many errors happened.
Follow a request ID through safe logs and traces. A request ID is a label that joins the clues for one trip.
Check recent changes and the slow part. Try one small fix, measure again, and keep a way to undo the change.

blocks.text: An **alert** asks a person to act. Base it on a useful problem, such as a sustained rise in failed loans. Too many alerts about tiny, harmless changes teach people to ignore them.
Handle missing data and private facts

If no requests arrive, the error percentage is not known from that window; dividing by zero is not useful. Our sample code assumes at least one request and one success. A real report must handle empty groups and show "no data".
Do not put passwords, access tokens, or unnecessary names into logs. Logs need access limits and a deletion schedule too. Keep enough detail to investigate without copying every private request.

items: Change the 110 ms request to ok: false. Keep the other values.
There are now two failures out of five: 40 percent. The three successful times add to 290 ms, so their average is about 96.67 ms. A lower successful average did not mean the service improved.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not report one average as proof that every user had a fast response. Show errors, slow waits, and the number of samples too.
